title: Lin et al. (2018): Multiple Choice
instructions: Choose the answer that best preserves the study design and model-specific findings. Distinguish odds, interval hazards, cumulative probabilities, and causal claims.

items.prompt: How is gray divorce defined for the couples studied?
options: Divorce after at least 50 years of marriage and after both spouses have retired
Divorce only when both spouses are over 50 and at least one has remarried
Divorce when at least one spouse is aged 50 or older
Divorce only in a first marriage when at least one spouse is 65 or older
items.answer: Divorce when at least one spouse is aged 50 or older
items.explanation: The study examines married couples with at least one spouse aged 50 or older. Neither a 50-year marriage nor retirement is required.

items.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the U.S. trend from 1990 to 2010?
options: The rate for married people aged 50+ doubled from 5 to 10 per 1,000 while the overall rate was fairly stable
The overall divorce rate doubled while the rate among married adults aged 50+ barely changed
The rate at ages 50-64 rose, but the rate at ages 65+ fell from 4.8 to 1.8 per 1,000
The overall and age-50-plus rates both declined by similar amounts during the same period
items.answer: The rate for married people aged 50+ doubled from 5 to 10 per 1,000 while the overall rate was fairly stable
items.explanation: These are historical annual rates among married people, not cumulative divorce probabilities. The rise in gray divorce occurred while the overall divorce rate remained comparatively stable.

items.prompt: Which description is inconsistent with the study's life-course approach?
options: Examining empty nest, retirement, and poor health as possible turning points in a marriage
Including marriage order, duration, teen marriage, and non-shared children as marital biography
Considering characteristics of both spouses together with their shared economic resources
Examining current transitions while excluding earlier marital history and both spouses' characteristics
items.answer: Examining current transitions while excluding earlier marital history and both spouses' characteristics
items.explanation: The approach combines later-life events with earlier trajectories, human agency, and linked lives. It uses couple-level information rather than treating current transitions in isolation.
items.source: How life-course ideas inform the design

items.prompt: Which pair gives the final sample and repeated observation count reported in the article?
options: 5,566 couples and 29,286 couple-interview-year observations
5,331 couples and 29,286 couple-interview-year observations
296 couples and 5,035 couple-interview-year observations
5,331 couples and 5,566 couple-interview-year observations
items.explanation: These are the article's reported final counts. The initial 5,566 and the four listed exclusion counts do not reconcile by simple subtraction, so the text does not provide a complete, arithmetically consistent sample flow.
items.source: Reported sample counts and the accounting limitation

items.prompt: Why were 218 remarriages to new spouses excluded?
options: All 218 couples had zero baseline weights and could not enter weighted estimates
All 218 were same-sex couples outside the study's selected population
All 218 were observed at only one wave and therefore lacked follow-up
To prevent a respondent from contributing another marriage after divorcing
items.answer: To prevent a respondent from contributing another marriage after divorcing
items.explanation: The restriction allowed each respondent to contribute only one marriage. Exclusions for same-sex couples, one-wave observations, and zero weights were listed separately.

items.prompt: How were the later-life transition variables coded for the analysis?
options: They equaled one only at the onset interview and returned to zero at the next wave
They used the status reported two years after the divorce interval being predicted
They stayed at one after onset and were lagged one interview wave before divorce
They were measured only at baseline and treated as fixed throughout follow-up
items.answer: They stayed at one after onset and were lagged one interview wave before divorce
items.explanation: Empty nest, each spouse's retirement, and each spouse's chronic-condition status were time-varying indicators that remained one after onset. A two-year lag established measured temporal ordering without proving causation.

options: Time together and enjoyment were combined and reverse-coded into separate spouse scores of 2-6
The spouses' responses were averaged into one couple score that was updated at every interview
Time together and conflict frequency formed separate baseline scores ranging from 2 to 6
Enjoyment alone was a time-varying 1-4 score without any measure of shared time
items.answer: Time together and enjoyment were combined and reverse-coded into separate spouse scores of 2-6
items.explanation: Higher scores represented more positive marital interaction. The questions were asked only at the couple's first interview, so wife and husband measures were entered separately as time-invariant covariates.

items.prompt: Why was discrete-time event-history analysis appropriate?
options: Exact daily divorce dates allowed continuous-time Cox hazards without interval information
Divorced couples remained in all subsequent risk sets to estimate repeated unconditional probabilities
It handles interval-observed events, changing covariates, risk sets, and censoring
It treats deaths and the end of follow-up as proof that a couple will never divorce
items.answer: It handles interval-observed events, changing covariates, risk sets, and censoring
items.explanation: The model estimates the probability of divorce in an interval conditional on no prior divorce. Observation can end before a future event occurs; the analysis is not simply a regression of lifetime cumulative probabilities.

options: After 40 years, cumulative probabilities for first marriages and remarriages converged at about .058
Remarriage probabilities rose earlier and remained nearly triple those of first marriages after 40 years
The remarriage value near .095 is the conditional hazard for a single interview interval
First-marriage probabilities rose earlier than remarriage probabilities and reached about .095
items.answer: Remarriage probabilities rose earlier and remained nearly triple those of first marriages after 40 years
items.explanation: The figure concerns cumulative gray-divorce probabilities. The near-zero early first-marriage curve partly reflects eligibility: many first marriages must last years before a spouse reaches 50. Long duration did not eliminate the marriage-order difference.
items.source: Cumulative probability and the observation design

items.prompt: What happened to the association between the wife's retirement and gray divorce across the two models?
options: It indicated about 43% higher odds in Model 1 and became nonsignificant in Model 2
It was absent in Model 1 but indicated about 43% lower odds after controls were added
It indicated lower odds in Model 1 and grew more strongly negative in Model 2
About 43% lower odds in Model 1 became nonsignificant in Model 2
items.answer: About 43% lower odds in Model 1 became nonsignificant in Model 2
items.explanation: The association did not persist after marital biography, marital quality, and sociodemographic factors were included. The result does not establish the wife's retirement as an independent causal protection against divorce.

items.prompt: Which statement matches the multivariate findings for remarriage and duration?
options: They correlated at -.69; only duration was significant jointly, while remarriage was significant without duration
They correlated at -.69 and both retained separate significant associations in the joint model
They correlated at +.69 and only remarriage was significant after both were included
They correlated at +.79 and neither was significant when examined in any model
items.answer: They correlated at -.69; only duration was significant jointly, while remarriage was significant without duration
items.explanation: Remarriages tend to be shorter, so the variables are strongly related. The joint model and the model omitting duration address different adjusted comparisons; the .79 correlation concerns non-shared children and remarriage.

items.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the heterogamy findings?
options: Only age difference was significant; racial and educational differences were unrelated to divorce
The interracial-couple odds ratio was 1.76; age and educational differences were not significant
The interracial odds ratio was 1.76 and age difference also had a significant positive association
Only educational difference was significant, while interracial couples did not have higher odds
items.answer: The interracial-couple odds ratio was 1.76; age and educational differences were not significant
items.explanation: Table 2 and the measurement definitions identify couples in which both spouses were White as the reference for the 1.76 odds ratio. This is more specific than comparing with all same-race couples, and an odds ratio is not a probability ratio.
items.source: Heterogamy and the actual reference category

items.prompt: Which account preserves the scope of the economic-resource findings?
options: Home ownership and wealth were associated with lower divorce odds and interpreted as barriers to separation
Home ownership predicted lower odds, but the wealth categories showed no differences
Wealth predicted lower odds while home ownership predicted higher odds
Debt alone was relevant; home ownership and wealth had no association in the models
items.answer: Home ownership and wealth were associated with lower divorce odds and interpreted as barriers to separation
items.explanation: The authors interpret economic security as a potential barrier to divorce. The observational associations do not prove that acquiring a house or assets would prevent divorce for a particular couple.

items.prompt: Which limitation matters when interpreting the nonsignificant marital-quality interactions?
options: Marital quality was updated so frequently that only immediate changes and no longer-term patterns were measured
Only wives answered the marital-quality questions, leaving husbands' experiences unavailable
Quality was measured only at the first interview, often years before a transition
Quality and every life transition were measured together at baseline with no later observations
items.answer: Quality was measured only at the first interview, often years before a transition
items.explanation: The fixed quality measure may miss changes shortly before or after empty nest, retirement, or illness. Absence of a significant interaction therefore does not establish that evolving relationship quality can never matter.

items.prompt: Which summary best captures the findings and proposed next steps?
options: The three transitions were the main risk factors, while marital history and quality were irrelevant
The wife's retirement remained an independent protective factor, ending the need for follow-up research
Only economic resources mattered, and adult children's post-divorce well-being was directly tested
Marital and economic factors mattered; consequences for divorcees and adult children remain research questions
items.answer: Marital and economic factors mattered; consequences for divorcees and adult children remain research questions
items.explanation: The fully adjusted findings gave little support to the three proposed turning points. The authors emphasize marital biography, quality, and resources and call for research on consequences, while acknowledging attrition, limited cohorts, and unmeasured marital processes.
